Alter
ôl'tər
v. (to change a thing from what it was; used of vows, decrees, and the word of God)
Latin alterare, to make other, from alter, another. The Hebrew shanah means to repeat or to change; the Chaldee of Ezra is the same root, used of tampering with a royal decree.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses alter almost exclusively for tampering with something that has been fixed, and the tone is always prohibitive. Of a devoted beast the law says, “He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy” (Lev 27:10) — a vow once made is not to be renegotiated, even upward. Darius protects the rebuilding of the temple with a decree against alteration and a penalty attached: “that shall put to their hand to alter and to destroy this house of God which is at Jerusalem” (Ezr 6:12). The Medo-Persian law was famous for it, and Daniel's enemies used the fact against him: the writing was signed “that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8). Then the word is lifted to its highest use, where God speaks of Himself: “My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” (Psa 89:34). Human decrees are unalterable by a legal fiction; God's word is unalterable by His nature.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to alter as to make some change in; to make different in some particular; to vary in some degree, without an entire change.

expand to see more

ALTER, v.t. [L. alter, another.] To make some change in; to make different in some particular; to vary in some degree, without an entire change.

2. To change entirely or materially; as, to alter an opinion.

ALTER, v.i. To vary; to change; to become different.

My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Ps. lxxxix.

Key Scripture

Lev 27:10 — "He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy."

Psa 89:34 — "My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."

Dan 6:8 — "Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not."

Mal 3:6 — "For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed."

Modern Corruption

The living church is now expected to alter the deposit it received in order to keep it credible, though Scripture attaches a curse to adding and diminishing and grounds our safety in a God who does not change.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy forbids adding to the word or diminishing ought from it, and Revelation closes the canon with the same double prohibition and a penalty. Both halves matter, because alteration usually presents itself as one or the other and rarely as both at once. Addition arrives as enrichment: a tradition, a practice, a further revelation, offered as completing what Scripture left bare. Diminishing arrives as candour: a doctrine quietly retired because it has become costly to hold — substitutionary punishment, eternal judgment, the created order of man and woman, the exclusiveness of Christ. Neither is a small correction of detail. The Authorized Version's use of the word is instructive here, because Leviticus 27:10 forbids exchanging the devoted beast a good for a bad, or a bad for a good. Even an improvement is forbidden. What has been given to God is not the giver's to revise.

Behind the prohibition stands the doctrine that makes the Christian faith stable at all. God says, I am the LORD, I change not, and the consequence He draws from it is not abstract but pastoral: therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. His immutability is the reason a covenant people survive their own inconstancy. Psalm 89 is the great instance, because the psalm is written in the middle of a disaster, its writer complaining that the crown has been cast to the ground, and it still records God saying He will not alter the thing gone out of His lips. That is the ground of assurance. If God could revise His word as men revise theirs, no promise could be leaned on for a decade, let alone an eternity; and Hebrews sets the same immutability in the Son — Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change or repeat; Chaldee shena (H8133), to alter, used of decrees in Ezra and Daniel; set against the divine lo shanithi, I change not, of Malachi 3:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change, to alter; he shall not alter it, nor change it; Leviticus 27:10.

Chaldee shena (H8133) — to alter or be changed; the decrees of Darius and of the Medes and Persians; Ezra 6:12, Daniel 6:8.

Hebrew shanah in Malachi 3:6 — I am the LORD, I change not; the immutability from which the mercy is drawn.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the thing God will not break nor alter; Psalm 89:34.

Greek aparabatos (G531) — unchangeable, not passing to another; used of Christ's unalterable priesthood; Hebrews 7:24.

Usage

"“He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good” — even an improvement forbidden."

"“Nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” — said in the middle of a disaster."

"“I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” — the doctrine and its comfort in one verse."
